game.name: Hand of Fate
game.short_description: Deckbuilding comes to life in Hand of Fate! An infinitely replayable series of quests - earn new cards, build your deck, then try to defeat it! In a cabin at the end of the world, the game of life and death is played. Draw your cards, play your hand, and discover your fate.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Hand of Fate (2015) is a deck-building roguelite that mixes a tabletop card-and-dealer layer with real-time 3D action combat. He likes the concept and especially the narrator, but feels the two halves clash. The card sections are slow and low on visual information, while the action part feels like a generic 3D brawler. He finds the fighting underwhelming and places it in the middle of C tier.
praise: The narrator/dealer voice and how he verbally explains everything is really cool
The concept of combining deck building with 3D action is appealing
He respects what the developers were going for
Some players could reasonably enjoy the contrast between the two styles
criticism: The card section is very slow paced
You see little on screen during the card part since the dealer just explains verbally
The action portion is a traditional 3D action game that feels like stock Unity-store assets
The two halves are drastically different from each other and do not blend well
unique_points: Card layer is presented as you sitting at a table with a narrating dealer rather than a UI of cards
Design lesson: games that fuse deck building with action often fall short because the two modes feel disconnected
commentary.quote: I like the idea so I'll put this as a like a like a mid C
comparisons: Other deck-building roguelites that combine card play with action
design_criteria: Genre fusion: whether deck building and action combine coherently
Pacing: card sections feel very slow
Combat feel: action fighting is underwhelming and generic
Presentation/charm: the narrator voice is a highlight, but assets feel stock
Information clarity: little visible on screen during card phases

community.one_liner: A 2015 hybrid from Defiant Development in which you play through randomly dealt card-based dungeon quests against a talking Dealer, with real-time third-person action combat whenever a fight card turns up.
community.consensus_summary: Hand of Fate is widely regarded as a distinctive, charming genre mash-up that predates Slay the Spire and helped seed the roguelike deckbuilder space. Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 89% of roughly 10,700 reviews), and critics landed at a Metacritic 78 on PC (79 PS4, 80 Xbox One), with user score 7.9. The Dealer, the card-driven storytelling and the unlock loop are loved; the simple Arkham-style combat, heavy RNG, repetition and a harsh final boss are the standing complaints. Many current players recommend it mainly on sale and say the sequel is the better entry, though some prefer the original's looser deckbuilding and flavor. It is a finished game (studio closed in 2019) and is not early access.
best_things: The Dealer: a menacing, talkative, witty narrator whose voice acting and banter are the glue of the game and the most-praised element
Original concept: a physical-feeling card table that generates the dungeon, events and shops, with the cards acting as the storytelling layer
Unlock loop: completing encounters awards tokens that unlock new equipment and encounter cards, so each run feels like it grows your deck and gives a sense of progress
Risk/reward encounters, where choices, dice, and gambles on the board can pay off or punish, and failure still yields unlocks
Atmosphere and presentation: beautiful card art, dark-fantasy tone, and a thematic soundtrack that reviewers called strong for an indie budget
Over-the-top, satisfying combat effects and slow-motion finishers for players who like a simple action layer
Accessible deckbuilding that lets you stuff in newly found cards and experiment without heavy optimization
Good value and a long tail for completionists (users report 20-190 hours chasing unlocks, endless mode and achievements)
worst_things: Combat is simplistic, Arkham-style button mashing with little depth, and many reviewers called it clunky, floaty or repetitive
Camera control is restrictive; players can be stuck with an angle that hides off-screen attacks and traps, both in combat and on the board
Heavy RNG: whether you assemble a workable kit before the boss can feel out of your control, and one reviewer alleges failed quests resurface more often
The final boss and final level are a sharp difficulty spike, described as a boss rush and unfair by several reviewers, and some never finished
Limited variety of encounters and enemies means the same fights and events repeat quickly
Jank and unpolished balance: unfixed bugs, inconsistent mouse/controller handling, endless-mode glitches, and uninterruptible attacks not clearly telegraphed
The Dealer's long lines and the slow card dealing animation grate on repeat runs
Marketing mismatch: several reviewers say it is an action game with cards as a storytelling layer, not a real card game or deckbuilder, so the roguelike-deckbuilder label disappoints
improvements: Make combat deeper with better telegraphs and readable distinction between interruptible and non-interruptible attacks
Add camera control, or at least a better fixed angle in combat and on the board
Give the player more agency over builds and RNG, with a smoother difficulty curve into the final boss
Allow skipping or speeding up the initial deal and repeated Dealer dialogue
More encounter and enemy variety, and a more meaningful post-campaign/endless mode beyond repeating runs for score
Clean up the achievement list, which players say is bloated with build-specific or pure-luck entries
unique_things: Two decks: one for equipment and one for the encounters that define the dungeon, so you literally choose the events you might face
A fusion of tabletop-style board progression with real-time action RPG combat, rare in its period
A personified adversary Dealer who narrates, taunts and reacts to your luck as the game master
Cards that both unlock and chain into follow-up encounters, weaving side quests into the main campaign through the deck
Predates Slay the Spire by about two years yet plays very differently from later roguelike deckbuilders, since cards are narrative and loadout rather than a combat hand
Spawned a physical companion board game (Hand of Fate: Ordeals) and a stronger sequel, and a new spin-off in the same universe is reported in development
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same encounters several times, sometimes with specific choices, to unlock certain upgrades
Early-game slog: several reviewers found the first half slow before it becomes engaging
Mashing through waves of swarming enemies, which feels repetitive and mindless to some
Endless mode after unlocking everything reduces to replaying similar runs for a better score
Long Dealer monologues and slow dealing animations that cannot be skipped easily
Grinding through RNG-dependent runs to land a viable build and non-crippling curses before the final boss
divisive_points: Combat: some enjoy the flashy, simple brawling as a fun counterpoint to the cards, while others call it the weakest part and overshadowing everything else
Dealer: loved by most as a charismatic villain, but a vocal minority find him an annoying over-talker
Deckbuilding: fans like its freedom and low barrier versus sequel's stricter approach, while critics call it too limited; some also object that it is not really a card game despite the marketing
Original vs sequel: many say Hand of Fate 2 is strictly better, others argue the first has more flavor and an easier, more brainless style they prefer
community.reception_notes: Launched February 2015 to generally favorable reviews (Metacritic PC 78 from 28 critics; user score 7.9 from 213 ratings) praising the concept and Dealer while noting slow pacing, repetitive combat and a hard final level. Wikipedia cites about 400,000 copies sold across platforms plus over 1.5 million downloads from an Xbox Live giveaway; SteamSpy lists 500k-1M Steam owners and the steam-revenue-calculator Boxleiter-style estimate is about $5.7M gross and $1.7M net on Steam (order-of-magnitude only; no copies figure given). Released on Windows, macOS, Linux, PS4 and Xbox One; a Vita version was cancelled. Hand of Fate 2 (Nov 2017) improved on it and outsold it over comparable periods. Defiant Development ceased operations in July 2019. Today the game has a low player count on Steam (single-digit concurrent players in our data) but remains well regarded; recent reviews commonly say to buy it on sale. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (search budget and site fetch failures), so it is left null.
